previews.html: Under Definition 2.7, the algorithm is a lower bound on the semantic delay: \mathrm{analyzeDelay}(\mathit{sys}) \leq \mathrm{delay}(\mathit{sys}, h)$$ The proof follows the inverse of the soundness strategy: symbolic witnesses are transported back to concrete ones using Definition 2.7 to pick distinct representatives trackedRep and backgroundRep for each branch label.
previews.label: analyzeDelay_le_delay
previews.title: Theorem 2.10

previews.html:
The reference symbolic delay algorithm. It enumerates all root configurations (reachable background state paired with one tracked symbolic input), then for each root configuration runs the system forward until the tracked packet exits or the bound is exceeded. The result is the maximum delay across all root configurations, or none (= ∞) if any root configuration has unbounded delay.

The computation is organized in two phases:

  1. Background reachability: compute all states reachable from initState under background-only traffic. The tracked packet arrives in some such state, so the worst case must quantify over all of them.

  2. Local delay: from each root configuration, explore reachable symbolic states and record the exit step of the tracked packet.
previews.label: analyze_delay
previews.title: Definition 2.4

previews.html:
If analyzeDelay sys = some d, then for every concrete packet type α, branching projection inspect : α → sys.branchingType, and input stream R, every packet entering at time t exits by time t + d.

The proof factors through three worlds.

World 1 — concrete (α): the goal is to bound the exit time of a specific concrete packet p entering at time t.

World 2 — symbolic Bool (branchingType × Bool): abstract the concrete execution to the symbolic one. The background state at time t is an abstract state reachable under false-traffic; the input at time t is turned into a root configuration with exactly one true packet.

World 3 — tagged transport (Sum α Unit): the technically subtle bridge. Two concrete packets a1, a2 might share a branch label (inspect a1 = inspect a2 but a1 ≠ a2), so α alone cannot tag one specific tracked packet. The fix: add a fresh marker Sum.inr () for the tracked packet and keep background packets as Sum.inl q.

One execution in the tagged world is read in two ways: projected to branchingType × Bool it provides the symbolic witness for the delay algorithm; projected back to α it gives the concrete certificate that p exits.
previews.label: analyze_delay_sound
previews.title: Theorem 2.5

previews.html:
The BFS that builds the explicit summary graph. Starting from the set of canonical root states (reachable plain states, each lifted to a tagged state with fresh tags), it maintains a queue of unprocessed states and a seen set:

  1. Dequeue a canonical state s.

  2. For each symbolic input i, run the device once at (s, i).

  3. Store the result as a StepSummary (output, delay estimate, successor state).

  4. Canonicalize the successor state; if unseen, enqueue it.

  5. Recurse until the queue is empty.

The result is a SummaryGraph: a mapping state ↦ List (input × StepSummary).
previews.label: build_summary_graph
previews.title: Definition 3.3

previews.html:
buildSummaryGraph is a terminating (non-partial) definition. Termination is witnessed by the strictly decreasing measure (\mathit{queue.size} - \mathit{head}) + (|\mathcal{U}| - |\mathit{seen} \cap \mathcal{U}|)$$ where \mathcal{U}$ is the finite bounded-canonical universe (boundedCanonUniverse). The first summand decreases when the queue is consumed; the second decreases when a new unseen state is discovered. The measure never increases because:

  • expandState_seen_subset: the seen set only grows.

  • expandState_queue_seen_delta: new queue entries are canonical states not yet in seen, so they reduce the second summand.

The bounded-canonical universe is finite by the packet-slot and bounded-tag lemmas proved in TaggedModel and Summary.
previews.label: build_summary_graph_termination
previews.title: Theorem 3.4

previews.html:
Three composition operators build networks from components.

  • Sequential seqComp sysL sysR (notation sysL ; sysR): the k outputs of sysL feed as the k inputs of sysR. The combined state is sysL.stateType × sysR.stateType.

  • Parallel parComp sys1 sys2 (notation sys1 + sys2): inputs split between sys1 and sys2; outputs concatenate. The combined state is a product.

  • Loop loopComp sys: for sys : system (n + k) (m + k), the last k outputs are fed back as the last k inputs at the next step, reducing to a system n m.

These operators let us build expressive network topologies compositionally while preserving a uniform one-step operational semantics.
previews.label: composition_operators

previews.title: Definition 1.3

previews.html:
The project instantiates the system interface with several concrete devices.

  • linkDelay D — a pure delay line that holds each packet for exactly D steps.

  • rateLimitedLink T — a 1-in/1-out link that emits at most one packet every T + 1 steps.

  • GCRA T τ — a Generic Cell Rate Algorithm / leaky-bucket shaper.

  • simplePriorityNode — a two-input, two-output non-preemptive priority scheduler.

  • splitter n / detSprayer n — 1-to-n packet distributors.

  • merger n C — n-to-1 merger with a bounded queue of capacity C.

  • tokenBucketFilter C K sizePacket — a token-bucket-style filter.

More complex examples include simplifiedFQCoDelCorrected (a simplified FQ-CoDel scheduler with bounded per-flow queues and new/old active lists) and the nonDetDelayer (a 1-to-n delay-tagged device parameterized by a maximum delay).

previews.html: Sequential composition satisfies an additive upper bound: \mathrm{delay}(L \,;\, R,\, h) \leq \mathrm{delay}(L,\, h_L) + \mathrm{delay}(R,\, h_R)$$ The bound is not tight in general; see Theorem 1.8.

previews.title: Theorem 1.7

previews.html:
A system n m is a stateful, packet-polymorphic device with n input links and m output links. Its four fields are:

  • stateType : Type → Type — the internal state, polymorphic in the packet type.

  • initState : stateType α — the initial state, natural with respect to packet maps.

  • branchingType : Type — the observable part of a packet used for routing decisions.

  • device : (α → branchingType) → statefulDevice α (stateType α) n m — the one-step transition, parameterized by an inspection function inspect : α → branchingType.

The key invariant is that the device may only observe packets through inspect. This separation between the concrete packet identity α and the routing label branchingType is what makes the symbolic delay analysis possible: two concrete packets with the same branch label are indistinguishable to the system.
previews.label: device_type
previews.parentTitle: Operational model of stateful packet-processing networks.
previews.title: Definition 1.1

previews.html:
The Enumerable typeclass provides a computable bijection between a type and Fin n for some n. It automatically derives DecidableEq, Fintype, and LinearOrder instances. It is the finiteness infrastructure used throughout the symbolic analysis to make state-space exploration executable.

The primary use is to constrain stateType and branchingType in a Definition 2.2: both must be Enumerable (after packet instantiation) for the delay algorithm to terminate.
previews.label: enumerable_class
previews.parentTitle: Key abstractions enabling finite symbolic exploration.
previews.title: Definition 2.1

previews.html:
A GoodSystem constrains a Definition 1.1 with four properties:

  1. State finiteness: stateType (branchingType × Bool) is Enumerable.

  2. Branching finiteness: branchingType is Enumerable.

  3. Functoriality: stateType is a Functor.

  4. Naturality: initState and device commute with packet maps.

Properties 3 and 4 are the critical ones for the proof. They ensure that changing the packet type during the proof does not break the connection between symbolic and concrete executions: packet maps commute with liftToStream, so symbolic runs and concrete runs can be rigorously compared.
previews.label: good_system
previews.parentTitle: Key abstractions enabling finite symbolic exploration.
previews.title: Definition 2.2

previews.html: Loop composition has no finite delay bound derivable from component delay alone. The device loopCE has delay = 0 (stateless, no buffering), yet \mathrm{delay}(\mathtt{loopComp}(\mathtt{loopCE})) = \top$$ A packet entering the feedback loop circulates forever, never reaching an external output. This rules out any bound delay (loopComp sys) ≤ f (delay sys) for any function f with f 0 < ⊤.
previews.label: loop_delay_infinite
previews.title: Theorem 1.10

previews.html:
If TwoInEveryFiber fails, the algorithm may return none (∞) even when the concrete delay is 0. The phantom-branch counterexample has branchingType = Fin 3 and α = Bool, with inspect false = 0, inspect true = 1. Branch 2 has an empty fiber — no concrete packet maps to it. Three facts hold simultaneously:

  • analyzeDelay phantomBranchCounterexample = none: the algorithm sees branch-2 tracked-packet configurations and never delivers them.

  • delayAtMost (α := Bool) phantomBranchCounterexample phantomInspect 0: every concrete packet exits immediately (branch 2 is unreachable concretely).

  • ¬ TwoInEveryFiber phantomInspect: the fiber of 2 is empty.

Failure mode: empty fiber — the algorithm chases ghost configurations that have no concrete instantiation.
previews.label: phantom_branch_counterexample
previews.title: Theorem 2.8

previews.html:
The priority-bypass counterexample shows that a singleton fiber suffices to break completeness. Here branchingType = Bool, α = Fin 3, with inspect {0,1} = false and inspect {2} = true. The true-fiber {2} is a singleton, violating Definition 2.7. Three facts hold:

  • analyzeDelay priorityBypassCounterexample = none: a tracked (true, true) packet in the buffer is indefinitely bypassed by background (true, false) packets.

  • delayAtMost (α := Fin 3) priorityBypassCounterexample surjInspect2 1: concretely, 2 in the buffer always exits at the next step regardless of the input.

  • ¬ TwoInEveryFiber surjInspect2.

Failure mode: singleton fiber — the algorithm treats (true, false) and (true, true) as distinct symbolic backgrounds, but concretely both map to 2.
previews.label: priority_bypass_counterexample
previews.title: Theorem 2.9

previews.html:
The semantic delay delay sys inspect : ℕ∞ is the worst-case time from packet arrival to packet exit, defined as a sup-of-inf over all streams and all packets: \mathrm{delay}(\mathit{sys}, h) = \sup_{R,\, t,\, p \in R_t} \inf \{\, \tau \mid p \text{ appears in output at } t + \tau \,\}$$ When the inner infimum ranges over an empty set (packet is never emitted), it equals ⊤, so packet loss and unbounded delay are unified semantically.

The predicate form delayAtMost sys inspect d says every packet entering at time t exits by time t + d. It is easier to work with inductively.
previews.label: semantic_delay
previews.title: Definition 1.5

previews.html: The additive bound Theorem 1.7 is strict in general. There exist systems seqCE_L (1-in/2-out, stateless) and seqCE_R (2-in/1-out) such that \mathrm{delay}(\mathtt{seqCE\_L} \,;\, \mathtt{seqCE\_R}) = 0 < 1 \leq \mathrm{delay}(\mathtt{seqCE\_L}) + \mathrm{delay}(\mathtt{seqCE\_R})$$ The mechanism: seqCE_L routes all traffic to port 0, so port 1 of seqCE_R is never used; but seqCE_R alone can buffer a port-1 arrival for one step. The composition never exercises that buffer path.
previews.label: seqcomp_delay_not_tight
previews.title: Theorem 1.8

previews.html:
The solved summary graph is semantically sound: if the fixed-point solver returns delay bound d for a query, then every concrete packet entering at time t exits by time t + d.

Status: in progress. The main missing bridge is completeness of the executable plain-state BFS: every reachablePlain state (a state semantically reachable from initState under plain inputs) belongs to computeReachablePlainStates sys (the array built by the BFS). Once this bridge is established, the concrete state at time t can be placed in rootSummaryStates, and the solver/query soundness argument can proceed.
previews.label: solved_summary_graph_sound
previews.title: Theorem 3.7

previews.html:
A system n m denotes a causal stream transformer from n input streams to m output streams. The one-step transition is iterated by liftToStream, which feeds the current input and state to the device, collects the output, and threads the successor state forward.

Streams are functions ℕ → Option α; a None at time t means no packet arrives on that link at step t. The k-stream type kStreams α k is a k-tuple of streams.
previews.label: stream_semantics

previews.title: Definition 1.2

previews.html:
The summary graph produced by taggedAnalyze is correct: for every reachable canonical state s and input i, the stored StepSummary correctly describes the one-step behavior of the device at (s, i).

The proof chain is: mkStepSummary_correct → computeStepSummary_correct → expandState_correctStateSummaries_aux → buildSummaryGraph_go_correct_aux → summaryGraphOfTaggedAnalyze_correct.
previews.label: summary_graph_correct
previews.title: Theorem 3.6

previews.html: After the BFS, the summary graph is solved by a Bellman-Ford-style fixed-point iteration (solveDelayTable). Starting from a zero delay table, it repeatedly propagates delay estimates through the stored StepSummary entries until the table stabilizes (early stopping). The final worst-case delay is then read off by queryWorstCaseDelay.
previews.label: summary_graph_solver
previews.title: Definition 3.5

previews.html:
The core idea of the symbolic analysis: replace concrete packets of type α by symbolic packets of type branchingType × Bool.

  • The branching label records everything the system may inspect.

  • The Bool tag distinguishes one tracked packet (true) from background traffic (false).

Because a Definition 2.2 has finitely many branch labels and the Bool tag adds one bit, the symbolic state space is finite. The algorithm can therefore terminate even though the original packet type α may be infinite.
previews.label: symbolic_packets
previews.title: Definition 2.3

previews.html:
In the tagged analysis, packets carry a Nat tag: the packet type is branchingType × Nat. The tag plays the role of the Bool in the symbolic analysis but allows finer distinction: distinct packets in the same fiber receive distinct natural-number tags. Canonicalization assigns tags in traversal order, producing canonical states that are unique up to packet identity.

Canonicalization: canonicalizeStateFull sys s renumbers all tags in a tagged state in traversal order, replacing each distinct tag with a fresh index starting from 0. This yields a canonical state whose tag list is determined by the plain state shape, not the original tag values.
previews.label: tagged_packets
previews.parentTitle: Interface and packet model for the tagged analysis.
previews.title: Definition 3.2

previews.html:
TaggedRunnable extends Definition 2.2 with Traversable support and two additional laws needed for the tagged BFS:

  1. Functor compatibility: the GoodSystem functor and the Traversable functor agree (goodSystemFunctor_eq_taggedFunctor).

  2. Reconstruction law: a tagged state is determined by its plain state together with its traversal-order tag list. This law is the key fact used in the termination proof.

TaggedRunnable is the single active interface for the tagged track. All concrete systems (nonDetDelayer, simplifiedFQCoDelCorrected, etc.) and system combinators (seqComp, parComp) carry TaggedRunnable instances.
previews.label: tagged_runnable
previews.parentTitle: Interface and packet model for the tagged analysis.
previews.title: Definition 3.1

previews.html: The completeness condition. TwoInEveryFiber inspect requires that every fiber of the inspection function inspect : α → β contains at least two distinct concrete packets: \forall b : \beta,\; \exists a_1 \neq a_2 : \alpha,\; \mathit{inspect}(a_1) = b \;\wedge\; \mathit{inspect}(a_2) = b$$ This is necessary because the Bool tag in the symbolic algorithm distinguishes the tracked packet from background by its tag bit — but two concrete packets with the same branch label are observationally identical to the system. If a fiber has only one element, there is no valid background representative, so the symbolic algorithm may chase configurations with no concrete instantiation.
previews.label: two_in_every_fiber
previews.title: Definition 2.7
